difficultyReason: The argument contains a two-level chain: evidence supports an intermediate conclusion (that antibiotic resistance is accelerated by agricultural overuse), which in turn supports the main conclusion (that regulations must cap agricultural antibiotic use). The target claim sits in the middle, and two answer choices each capture only one of its dual functions.
stimulus: Agricultural overuse of antibiotics now accounts for the majority of antibiotic consumption in most industrialized nations. Because bacteria exposed repeatedly to sub-therapeutic doses of antibiotics develop resistance far more rapidly than bacteria exposed only in clinical settings, agricultural overuse is the primary driver of the accelerating resistance crisis. Therefore, any serious policy effort to preserve antibiotic efficacy must include binding caps on their agricultural use.
questionStem: The claim that agricultural overuse is the primary driver of the accelerating resistance crisis plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the observation that bacteria exposed to sub-therapeutic doses develop resistance more rapidly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the main conclusion, with no support provided for it within the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from evidence about bacterial resistance development, and it is itself used to support the main conclusion about policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is background context establishing the scale of agricultural antibiotic consumption, rather than a logically operative claim.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a position the argument acknowledges only to set aside in favor of a broader explanation of the resistance crisis.

explanations.correct: The claim is an intermediate conclusion: it is supported by the preceding evidence about sub-therapeutic dosing and rapid resistance development, and it then functions as the key premise licensing the 'therefore' conclusion about binding policy caps. Choice C captures both functions.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the policy claim (binding caps must be included). Calling this claim the main conclusion ignores the 'therefore' that introduces the policy statement — this is the 'confuses intermediate conclusion with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The claim is not unsupported within the argument; the sub-therapeutic dosing evidence supports it. Calling it a bare premise misses its conclusion function — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The claim is not mere background; it does logical work as a step in the argument's inferential chain. This is the 'background vs. support' trap.
explanations.E: The argument never acknowledges an alternative explanation and sets it aside; this describes a concession-rebuttal structure that is absent here.

difficultyReason: The argument deploys a three-step chain in an economics context. The target claim — that consumer confidence, not interest rates, drives discretionary spending — is an intermediate conclusion drawn from survey data and used to support the main conclusion that rate cuts alone cannot revive a stagnant economy.
stimulus: Central bank surveys show that households consistently cite job-security concerns as the primary reason for curtailing discretionary purchases, even when borrowing costs are at historic lows. This indicates that consumer confidence, not interest rates, is the dominant determinant of discretionary spending. Consequently, a central bank that responds to economic stagnation solely by cutting rates is deploying the wrong instrument for the problem it faces.
questionStem: The claim that consumer confidence, not interest rates, is the dominant determinant of discretionary spending plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the survey findings and the critique of rate-cutting policy both serve as support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an unsupported assumption the argument presupposes but does not defend.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the survey data, and it in turn supports the main conclusion that rate cuts alone are the wrong policy instrument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a concession to the view that interest rates matter, which the argument subsequently overturns.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a general economic principle cited to explain why the survey findings are reliable.

explanations.correct: The claim is supported by the survey data (households cite job-security concerns even at low rates) and itself supports the 'consequently' conclusion that rate cuts are the wrong instrument. It is a textbook intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is introduced by 'consequently' and concerns policy (rate cuts as wrong instrument). Treating the spending-determinant claim as the main conclusion misreads the argument's architecture — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The claim is explicitly supported by the survey evidence, so it is not unsupported. This is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.
explanations.D: The claim does not concede anything to the view that interest rates matter; it directly contradicts that view using evidence. There is no subsequent reversal — this is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does not explain why the survey findings are reliable; causally the survey findings explain the claim, not the reverse.

difficultyReason: An ethics argument about whistleblower protection uses a three-step inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing act in the public interest — is supported by a premise about democratic accountability and itself supports the main conclusion about legal protection. Trap choices isolate only one of its two roles.
stimulus: Democratic accountability requires that citizens have access to accurate information about the conduct of powerful institutions. Employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing are often the only available source of such information; hence, they act in the public interest when they make such disclosures. It follows that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing in good faith deserve robust legal protection from retaliation.
questionStem: The claim that employees who disclose organizational wrongdoing act in the public interest plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the claims about democratic accountability and the uniqueness of employee disclosures as information sources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, and no support is given for it in the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an opposing view that the argument ultimately rejects in favor of a narrower conception of employee obligations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by evidence about democratic accountability and employees' unique informational role, and it is itself used to support the conclusion about legal protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context that motivates the argument without functioning as a logical step in the inferential chain.

explanations.correct: The claim follows ('hence') from the premises about democratic accountability and employees' unique role as information sources, and it then licenses ('it follows that') the main conclusion about legal protection. It is an intermediate conclusion, and D accurately captures both its supported and supporting functions.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is about legal protection, introduced by 'it follows that.' Treating the public-interest claim as the main conclusion is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The claim is supported within the argument by two preceding premises, so it cannot be characterized as unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.C: The argument nowhere treats this claim as an opposing view; it affirmatively defends it. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative logical work as an intermediate step; calling it mere background misclassifies its function — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.

difficultyReason: An environmental science argument about carbon sequestration features a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than forests can absorb it — is supported by comparative flux data and supports the main conclusion that wetland preservation must take priority over reforestation in climate policy.
stimulus: Measurements of carbon flux show that degraded peatlands emit roughly ten times more carbon per hectare annually than equivalent areas of temperate forest absorb. Given these figures, peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than reforestation efforts can compensate. Therefore, climate policy that prioritizes new tree planting over peatland preservation is systematically misdirected.
questionStem: The claim that peatland degradation is releasing sequestered carbon faster than reforestation efforts can compensate plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, with no inferential support provided for it within the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the carbon-flux measurements serve as evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from carbon-flux data, and it functions as the key premise supporting the main conclusion about policy priorities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a concession acknowledging the limits of peatland preservation that the argument then reframes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is contextual information explaining what carbon sequestration is, rather than a logically operative claim.

explanations.correct: The claim is supported by the carbon-flux measurement data ('given these figures') and then supports the 'therefore' conclusion about policy. Both functions are captured by C, identifying it as an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The argument does provide inferential support for the claim (the flux measurements). Calling it an unsupported premise is the 'partial function' trap — it misses the conclusion role.
explanations.B: The main conclusion is the policy claim introduced by 'therefore.' Treating this as the main conclusion is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.D: No concession structure exists here; the argument never acknowledges a contrary view about peatland preservation. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not definitional background; it is a substantive inferential step. This is the 'background vs. support' trap.

difficultyReason: A technology argument about algorithmic content moderation uses a three-step chain. The intermediate conclusion — that automated moderation systems cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement — is supported by empirical error-rate data and used to support the main conclusion that platforms should not rely solely on automated moderation for political content.
stimulus: Error-rate analyses of major platforms' automated moderation systems show that these systems misclassify satirical political content as incitement at rates exceeding forty percent. Automated moderation systems therefore cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement. Platforms that rely exclusively on such systems for political content thus risk systematically suppressing protected speech, which means they must incorporate human review for any content flagged in political categories.
questionStem: The claim that automated moderation systems cannot reliably distinguish political satire from sincere incitement plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the error-rate analysis and the risk of suppressing protected speech both serve as support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by error-rate data, and it in turn supports the conclusion that platforms risk suppressing protected speech, which itself supports the main conclusion about human review.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, with no inferential basis provided for it within the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a position the argument attributes to critics of automated moderation but does not itself endorse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context about the technical limitations of machine learning, introduced to frame the subsequent policy recommendation.

explanations.correct: The argument is a three-step chain: error-rate data → (intermediate 1) automated systems cannot reliably distinguish satire from incitement → (intermediate 2) platforms risk suppressing protected speech → (main conclusion) platforms must incorporate human review. The target claim is the first intermediate conclusion, supported by data and supporting the next link. B captures this.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the requirement for human review. The target claim is an intermediate step, not the endpoint — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: The error-rate data provides inferential support for the target claim, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument endorses this claim; it does not attribute it to critics. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative inferential work; it is not mere framing background — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.

difficultyReason: A linguistics argument about language extinction turns on an intermediate conclusion — that the loss of a language entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions encoded in it — which is derived from fieldwork evidence and used to support the main conclusion that language preservation warrants dedicated institutional funding.
stimulus: Linguistic fieldwork consistently documents that many endangered languages encode spatial, temporal, and kinship distinctions for which no equivalent expressions exist in dominant languages. The loss of such a language therefore entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions that cannot be reconstructed from surviving records. Accordingly, language preservation programs deserve the same category of institutional support that is routinely granted to the preservation of unique biological species.
questionStem: The claim that the loss of such a language entails the loss of irreplaceable conceptual distinctions plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the fieldwork findings about untranslatable distinctions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion, for which no support is provided in the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion the argument draws from fieldwork evidence, and it functions as the premise supporting the institutional-funding conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the argument concedes to critics of language preservation before rebutting it with the fieldwork data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a general principle used to evaluate competing claims about the relative merits of biological versus linguistic preservation.

explanations.correct: The claim follows ('therefore') from the fieldwork evidence about untranslatable distinctions and itself supports ('accordingly') the main conclusion about institutional funding. C correctly identifies both its supported and supporting functions — it is an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the institutional-funding claim, introduced by 'accordingly.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The fieldwork evidence does support the target claim within the argument, so calling it unsupported is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: No concession-rebuttal structure exists; the argument never attributes this claim to critics. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not a general evaluative principle; it is a specific empirical-inferential step about what language loss entails. This is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.

difficultyReason: A history argument about the decline of the Roman Western Empire uses a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that the economic contraction of the third century fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to field professional armies — is drawn from fiscal evidence and used to support the main conclusion that military overextension alone cannot explain the empire's collapse.
stimulus: Papyrological records from the third century CE document a severe contraction in tax revenues collected across western provinces, coinciding with currency debasement and a collapse of long-distance trade networks. This economic contraction fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to fund and sustain professional armies along its borders. Attributing Rome's eventual collapse solely to military overextension therefore ignores the deeper fiscal deterioration that had already undermined the very instrument of that military capacity.
questionStem: The claim that the economic contraction fundamentally weakened the empire's capacity to fund and sustain professional armies plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the papyrological records and the critique of military overextension accounts both serve as evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise for which no support is offered in the argument, used to refute the military-overextension explanation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the fiscal evidence, and it is itself used to support the main conclusion that military overextension alone cannot explain Rome's collapse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a concession the argument makes to proponents of the military-overextension thesis before arguing that both factors are equally important.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background historical context establishing the chronological setting for the main argument.

explanations.correct: The papyrological fiscal evidence supports the target claim, and the target claim then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion that military overextension alone is insufficient as an explanation. C captures both inferential roles correctly.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the anti-reductionist thesis about military overextension, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The papyrological records provide explicit support for the target claim within the argument, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not concede that military overextension is equally important; it argues fiscal factors are the deeper cause. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not mere chronological context; it does substantive inferential work as the intermediate conclusion — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.

difficultyReason: A law argument about prosecutorial disclosure obligations features a two-level chain. The intermediate conclusion — that withholding forensic evidence favorable to the defense compromises the fairness of criminal proceedings — is derived from due-process principles and used to support the main conclusion that courts should impose automatic reversals when such evidence is concealed.
stimulus: Due process requires that criminal proceedings be genuinely adversarial, which in turn demands that each side have meaningful access to the evidence bearing on guilt or innocence. When prosecutors withhold forensic evidence favorable to the defense, that requirement is violated, and the fairness of the proceedings is fundamentally compromised. Courts should therefore treat such concealment as grounds for automatic reversal of any conviction obtained in those proceedings, without requiring the defendant to demonstrate prejudice from the specific omission.
questionStem: The claim that the fairness of the proceedings is fundamentally compromised plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, supported by the due-process principle and the observation that prosecutorial concealment violates adversarial requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from due-process principles and the violation of adversarial requirements, and it supports the main conclusion that courts should impose automatic reversals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an unsupported premise the argument assumes in order to justify automatic reversals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view endorsed by critics of prosecutorial misconduct rules that the argument evaluates but ultimately finds insufficient.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a general legal principle invoked to clarify what due process requires, rather than a substantive inferential step.

explanations.correct: The target claim follows from the due-process principle and the observation that adversarial requirements are violated when evidence is withheld. It then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion about automatic reversals. B correctly identifies it as an intermediate conclusion serving both functions.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the automatic-reversal rule, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: The due-process principle and the adversarial-requirement violation provide support for the target claim; it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not attribute this claim to critics; it affirmatively asserts it. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim is not merely clarifying what due process requires; it is a substantive conclusion about the effects of prosecutorial concealment — this is the 'accurate content, wrong function' trap.

difficultyReason: An arts-policy argument about public funding for experimental theater uses a three-step chain. The intermediate conclusion — that experimental theater generates aesthetic innovations later adopted by commercial productions — is supported by historical examples and used to support the main conclusion that public funding for experimental theater produces broad cultural benefits, not merely niche ones.
stimulus: Historical records show that staging techniques now standard in commercial theater — including thrust stages, non-realistic lighting, and ensemble-devised scripts — were pioneered by publicly funded experimental companies in the mid-twentieth century. Experimental theater thus generates aesthetic innovations that commercial productions eventually adopt and disseminate to broad audiences. Public funding for experimental theater therefore produces cultural benefits far beyond the small audiences who attend experimental performances directly, and this breadth of benefit justifies substantial public subsidy.
questionStem: The claim that experimental theater generates aesthetic innovations that commercial productions eventually adopt and disseminate to broad audiences plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: The historical staging-technique examples support ('thus') the target claim, and the target claim then supports ('therefore') the main conclusion about breadth of cultural benefit justifying subsidy. C correctly identifies both its supported and supporting functions as an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the justification for substantial public subsidy, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.B: The historical records do provide support for the target claim; it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.D: The argument does not attribute the claim to advocates of commercial theater; it derives it from historical evidence. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.

difficultyReason: A policy argument about urban heat-island mitigation uses a two-level inferential chain. The intermediate conclusion — that dark impervious surfaces in dense urban areas absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures — is drawn from thermal imaging data and used to support the main conclusion that municipal building codes should mandate reflective roofing materials.
stimulus: Thermal imaging surveys of major cities consistently show that surface temperatures in densely built neighborhoods exceed those of surrounding rural areas by as much as eight degrees Celsius, even when ambient weather conditions are identical. Dark impervious surfaces in such neighborhoods absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures — a finding that directly follows from the thermal imaging data. Municipal building codes should therefore mandate reflective roofing and paving materials in high-density zones, since doing so would reduce the heat retention responsible for these dangerous temperature differentials.
questionStem: The claim that dark impervious surfaces in such neighborhoods absorb and retain heat in ways that significantly elevate local temperatures plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered directly in support of the main conclusion about building codes, with no supporting evidence provided for it in the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the thermal imaging data and the policy recommendation both serve as evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a concession to urban planners who dispute the degree to which surface materials affect local temperatures, which the argument then rebuts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion supported by the thermal imaging data, and it serves as the key premise supporting the main conclusion that building codes should mandate reflective materials.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background scientific information explaining the urban heat-island phenomenon, offered to orient the reader rather than to support any specific policy claim.

explanations.correct: The argument states that the heat-absorption claim 'directly follows from the thermal imaging data,' establishing its supported role. It then underlies ('therefore') the mandate for reflective materials, establishing its supporting role. D correctly identifies it as an intermediate conclusion serving both functions.
explanations.A: The thermal imaging data explicitly supports the target claim within the argument, so it is not unsupported — this is the 'partial function' trap.
explanations.B: The main conclusion is the building-code mandate, introduced by 'therefore.' The target claim is an intermediate step — this is the 'confuses intermediate with main conclusion' trap.
explanations.C: No concession-rebuttal structure involving urban planners exists; the argument presents this as an affirmative finding. This is the 'opposing view confusion' trap.
explanations.E: The claim does operative inferential work connecting the data to the policy conclusion; it is not mere background orientation — this is the 'background vs. support' trap.
